title: The health sweep stops enumerating a retired environment
description:
SPIDR child 2 of task-de80c663569a4ab2b30a9db6ac526e4b, split by architect-5385678f 2026-09-08. dependsOn child 1 (task-a2dd124fed1b4b9889c626824fc0a6fb), the retirement record this row reads.

OBJECTIVE. Make the sweep honour the retirement fact. This is the half of the parent's DoD 1 that says "createHealthProbeJob stops enumerating it: a probe tick after retirement records no sample for that name".

THE DEFECT, measured at HEAD by worker-bcaa6d5e: `apps/daemon/src/monitoring/health-probe-ring.ts:240 createHealthProbeJob` enumerates what to probe as `[...readDeployLedger(options.store, options.projectId).keys()].filter(name => !skip.has(name))`. `readDeployLedger` derives its environment set from DEPLOY RECEIPTS, which are append-only, so an environment enters the sweep on its first deploy and can never leave it.

THE MECHANISM ALREADY EXISTS AND MUST BE REUSED, NOT REBUILT. That same line already honours a `dedicated` skip set supplied as a callback and READ PER TICK — its comment at :237-239 says so, and `daemon-store-foundation-composition.ts:670` supplies it from `probeIntervals.stored()`. Retirement is the same shape with a different source. Follow it: a per-tick read, no restart required, empty by default so the shipped behaviour is unchanged when nothing is retired.

DELIVERABLE WHEN DONE: `createHealthProbeJob` excludes retired environments, and `daemon-store-foundation-composition.ts` constructs the child-1 record ONCE (as it already does for `probeIntervals` at :641) and supplies the predicate to the sweep. `createEnvironmentHealthProbeJob` should be considered too — an environment with a dedicated interval that is then retired must stop probing on BOTH paths, and its `active()` predicate at :250-252 is where that belongs.

NOT IN SCOPE: no command kind, no vocabulary or digest-mirror change (child 3), no daemon command edge (child 4). Nothing can WRITE a retirement when this row lands — the arms drive the record directly, which is exactly how the interval arms in health-probe-io.test.ts already work.

WHY THIS ROW LANDS BEFORE THE COMMAND, and it is a safety ordering rather than paperwork: if child 4 landed first, an operator could retire an environment and the sweep would keep probing it — the product would advertise a capability that does not work. Reader before writer.

VERIFICATION COMMAND: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test` — FOREGROUND and STANDALONE, quote the `Test Files N passed` count line, not just the exit code.
definitionOfDone: createHealthProbeJob excludes environments the child-1 record reports retired, read PER TICK like the existing dedicated skip set, with no restart required.
A probe tick after retirement records NO new sample for the retired name: asserted by reading the ring before and after the tick, not by inspecting the enumerated list.
A dedicated per-environment job for a retired environment also stops probing, so retirement is not escapable by owning an interval.
Default behaviour is unchanged: with nothing retired, the sweep enumerates exactly what it enumerates today, asserted by an arm.
The retired environment's existing ring samples and deploy receipts stay readable after the tick.
pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test EXIT 0 with its Test Files count line quoted.

THEN READ THE THREE PLACES THIS ROW TOUCHES, because the mechanism already exists and this row extends it rather than inventing anything:
- health-probe-ring.ts:237-244 — `createHealthProbeJob(options, dedicated)`. The `dedicated` callback is READ PER TICK inside the returned job, which is why setting or clearing an interval needs no restart. Its comment says exactly that. Retirement is the same shape from a different source.
- health-probe-ring.ts:249-252 — `createEnvironmentHealthProbeJob(options, environment, active)`, whose `active()` predicate is also read per tick and already returns `[]` when false.
- daemon-store-foundation-composition.ts:641-670 — `probeIntervals` is constructed ONCE at :641, `dedicated()` at :649 reads `probeIntervals.stored()` on every call and yields the EMPTY set when the store cannot answer ("never no probing at all"), `dedicatedJob` at :652 composes the per-environment predicate, `reconcileProbeSchedules` at :662 arms schedules from the interval record, and `sweepProbe` at :670 wires it all together.

NOTE THE FAIL-OPEN CONVENTION AT :649 AND DECIDE ITS RETIREMENT ANALOGUE DELIBERATELY, because the two facts fail in OPPOSITE directions. An unreadable interval record yields the empty set, which hands every environment back to the sweep — fail-open is right there, since the cost is probing at the default rate. An unreadable RETIREMENT record yielding the empty set means probing environments that may be retired, which is the defect this row fixes; yielding "everything retired" means probing NOTHING, which is worse. State which you chose and why in a comment. There is no free answer here — make it a decision, not an accident.

implementationPlan.description:
WIRE IT, AND CLOSE THE DEDICATED-JOB ESCAPE — daemon-store-foundation-composition.ts.

(1) Construct the child-1 retirement record ONCE alongside `probeIntervals` at :641, and add a `retired()` callback beside `dedicated()` at :649 that reads its snapshot on every call. One instance, not one per call — daemon-command-registry.ts:547 ("THE ONE PORT, SHARED") states the reason on the sibling edge, and child 4 will need the SAME instance so a retirement takes effect on the next tick rather than at the next restart.

(2) Pass `retired` to `createHealthProbeJob` at :670.

(3) CLOSE THE ESCAPE. `dedicatedJob` at :652 gives a per-environment job whose `active()` is `dedicated().has(environment)`. An environment that owns an interval is served by THAT job, not by the sweep — so excluding it from the sweep alone leaves it probing forever. Compose retirement into that predicate too, so a retired environment stops on BOTH paths. This is DoD 3 and it is the clause a partial fix fails.

(4) DECIDE `reconcileProbeSchedules` (:662) DELIBERATELY. It iterates the interval record and calls `schedules.register(…)` for every entry, so a retired environment that still holds an interval keeps a schedule ARMED whose job now probes nothing. That satisfies "records no sample", but epic rail 4 is explicit — anything this epic starts, it stops — and an armed timer that can never fire usefully is something started and not stopped. PREFERRED: skip arming retired environments there. If you leave it armed, say why in a comment; do not leave it unexamined.

Do not change the reconcile-before-sweep ordering at :672-675 or its comment — it exists so an environment that just gained an interval is not probed twice on the way to being right, and that reasoning is untouched by retirement.

implementationPlan.description:
THE ARMS — ASSERT THE RING, NOT THE ROSTER (DoD 1, 2, 4, 5).

In health-probe-io.test.ts, following the existing sweep arms at :146-159 (which `deploy(…)` two environments, run `createHealthProbeJob`, and assert `fixture.ring.read(<name>)`):

(a) THE SUBJECT. Deploy two environments, retire one, run ONE tick, and assert the retired name's ring is UNCHANGED across the tick while the other gained a sample. Read the ring BEFORE and AFTER and compare — DoD 2 says this explicitly, and it matters: asserting the enumerated list would pass against a filter that excludes the name from enumeration while some other path still probes it. The ring is the fact an operator sees; assert the fact.

(b) PER-TICK, NO RESTART. Run a tick, THEN retire, THEN run a second tick against the SAME job instance, and assert the second tick recorded nothing new. This is what proves the callback is read per tick rather than captured at construction — a job that captured the set at build time passes (a) and fails this.

(c) DEFAULT UNCHANGED (DoD 4). With nothing retired, the sweep enumerates and probes exactly what it does today. Without this arm, a filter that excluded everything would pass (a) and (b).

(d) HISTORY SURVIVES (DoD 5). The retired environment's EXISTING ring samples are still readable after the tick, and its deploy receipts still read back through `readDeployLedger`. Assert content, not merely that the call returned — a reader that silently answers empty would pass a shallow check.

In health-probe-schedule.test.ts, the neighbour that already covers the dedicated/reconcile path:
(e) THE ESCAPE IS CLOSED (DoD 3). A dedicated per-environment job for a retired environment probes NOTHING — drive `createEnvironmentHealthProbeJob` with the composed predicate from step 3 and assert its ring is unchanged across a tick.

Assert on ring CONTENT throughout. `expect(ring.read(name)).toEqual({ ok: true, value: […] })` is the idiom already in this file; keep it.

🧭 GOVERNOR NOTE FOR QA — one piece of this row's evidence is not admissible, and the row is otherwise fine. governor-74f24573, 2026-09-09T10:15Z. @qa-01b7fe3f you claimed at 10:13:57Z, 25s before I posted this in chat, so you may not have seen it.

**DO NOT ACCEPT AN EMPTY `git diff` AS THIS ROW'S RESTORE PROOF.** Step 5 instructs it explicitly:

> "all four are TRACKED, so an empty `git diff -- <path>` is a valid restore proof, taken in a call SEPARATE from the restore."

**That inverts on this row.** The drill targets carry the row's own uncommitted implementation:
```
git status --porcelain -- apps/daemon/src/monitoring/
 M health-probe-io.test.ts
 M health-probe-ring.ts
 M health-probe-schedule.test.ts
```
For a file the row has modified, an empty `git diff` means the file matches **HEAD** — i.e. **the implementation was discarded**, not restored. A `git checkout -- <path>` after a mutation produces exactly that state and exactly that green proof. The step's reasoning picks the wrong property: *tracked* is not what makes the proof valid, **clean** is.

**THE BYTES ARE INTACT — I measured, so this is a note about the evidence, not a defect claim:**
```
health-probe-ring.ts:243   retired: () => ReadonlySet<string> = () => new Set()
health-probe-ring.ts:246   const excluded = retired();
git diff --stat            45 insertions, 5 deletions across the two files
```
The worker appears to have restored from a copy or drilled process-locally rather than via `git checkout --`. **That is an inference — I did not observe which**, only that the deliverable survived.

**WHAT I AM ASKING OF YOU:** verify the implementation on its merits rather than through that proof — the `retired` callback threaded into `createHealthProbeJob` and its exclusion applied at the enumeration, plus the arms actually failing when the exclusion is removed. A restore proof that would read identically whether the work is present or deleted tells you nothing either way.

**NOT A REJECTION SIGNAL.** The worker did not do anything wrong; it followed an approved step. If the deliverable verifies, approve it. The defect is in the plan wording, and it matters because the next row that copies that sentence will not necessarily be lucky — the failure mode is silent, with a green proof over deleted work.

For future drill steps, the rule that holds either way: hash the **live** file at window-open, restore from a copy, and prove by SHA256 equality in a separate call. Reserve empty-`git diff` for files the row never touched.

Mode "after first tick" constructs the job, ticks, retires, then ticks the SAME instance — that is the arm a construction-time capture fails while "before construction" still passes.
3. daemon-store-foundation-composition.ts:662 — `dedicatedJob`'s predicate is `dedicated().has(env) && !retired().has(env)`, and :755 `resolveProbe` applies the same exclusion at restore. health-probe-schedule.test.ts:235 mode "dedicated" drives the REAL composition through `createStoreDependencies`: staging holds a 10s interval, is retired, and 60s of advance (six dedicated ticks plus one sweep tick) leaves its ring byte-identical. The escape is closed on both paths.
4. Mode "default unchanged" passes `undefined` for `retired` and asserts a NEW sample IS appended to both environments — this is what stops an over-broad filter passing every other arm.
5. `expect(before.value[0]).toEqual(SAMPLE)` pins historical ring content, and `expect(readDeployLedger(...)).toEqual(ledger)` asserts the WHOLE ledger map by equality, not merely that the read returned.
6. Above.

RAILS CHECKED. Reason-code rail satisfied: the fail-direction arm corrupts the aggregate and asserts the exact `{ok:false, code:"ENVIRONMENT_RETIREMENT_RECORD_INVALID", layer:"DAEMON_INGRESS"}`, not merely "refused". Fail direction was chosen deliberately and documented at :654-656 (unreadable record yields no exclusions, so a retired URL may be probed rather than every live environment going blind) — the architect required a decision, not an inherited copy-paste, and got one. Epic rail 4 (anything started is stopped): `reconcileProbeSchedules` now skips ARMING retired entries, the architect's stated preference, and the residual pre-existing arms are documented at :660-662 as inert reactivation watchers with the reason the scheduler has no scoped stop; the arm asserts `timer.arms.length - arms === 1` and `liveIntervals() === [DEFAULT]` across a reboot, so nothing re-arms retired.

SCOPE ADDITION I EXAMINED AND ACCEPTED. :787-789 narrows the durable-schedule resolver so reserved probe ids never fall through to `config.schedule.resolve`. Not literally in the plan, but it closes a real resurrection hole (a permissive external resolver could re-arm a retired probe at restore) and the new fallback-counting resolver in the schedule fixture exercises it. I checked the one existing external-resolver test, daemon-store-dependencies.test.ts:1319, and it registers id "unrelated" — `healthProbeJobEnvironment` returns null for that, so it still falls through and still asserts `externalCalls === 1`. No regression.

ADVERSARIAL: THIRD ENUMERATING PATH. I grepped every non-test `readDeployLedger(` caller. Besides health-probe-ring.ts:247 the callers are affordance-rollback-offers.ts:83, goal-deployment-read.ts:49, runs-read.ts:176, deploy-ledger.ts's own accessors, and the retirement record itself — all operator-facing READ surfaces, none of which probe. No fourth path needs the same exclusion.

READER WITH NO WRITER. Confirmed and correct: nothing can write a retirement until child 4 (task-1714234a) lands, so this row is observably inert on its own. The arms drive `record.write` directly, which is how the interval arms already work. Reader-before-writer is the safety ordering the description names, and I am NOT treating the inertness as untested.

FOLLOW-UP, NOT A REJECTION. `daemon-store-foundation-composition.ts` is 857 physical lines, over the 400 split threshold — but it was already 841 at HEAD before this diff, and this row added 16 lines of which most are the doc comments the plan explicitly required. Pre-existing debt, not introduced here, and splitting an 841-line composition file is its own row. Recording it here per the delivery-bias rail rather than filing a row. Also for whoever holds child 4: `probeRetirements` at :643 is a module-local const with no accessor on the returned dependencies, so child 4 will need to expose that SAME instance rather than constructing a second one — the "ONE PORT, SHARED" reason the plan cited still has to be honoured at that edge.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
REJECTED — fold retirement into the existing `dedicated` skip set in the composition, changing NO production line in health-probe-ring.ts. It is the smallest possible diff and it works mechanically: the sweep already excludes that set per tick, and `reconcileProbeSchedules` iterates the interval record rather than the skip set, so no schedule would be wrongly armed. Rejected because the parameter is NAMED `dedicated` and its comment defines it as "environments that own a job at their own interval" — a retired environment with no interval is not that. The code would be right and the name would lie, and the next person to touch it fixes the wrong thing. Two facts, two sources.

REJECTED — filter inside `probeJob` or `probeEnvironment`. Wrong altitude: `probeJob`'s comment states that the environment SOURCE is the only axis its two constructors differ on, and pushing a policy filter down into the shared prober would apply it to callers that never asked for it.

REJECTED — have the sweep read the retirement record directly instead of taking a callback. It would bind health-probe-ring.ts to a specific record module, where today it takes a plain `() => ReadonlySet<string>` and is testable without any store fixture. The callback shape is the existing contract; keep it.

REJECTED — asserting the enumerated environment list rather than the ring. It is the easier assertion and it is weaker: a filter that excludes a name from enumeration while some other path still probes it would pass. DoD 2 says ring-before-and-after for exactly this reason.

CONSIDERED, LEFT TO THE WORKER WITH A STATED PREFERENCE — whether `reconcileProbeSchedules` should also skip ARMING a schedule for a retired environment that still holds an interval. Its job's `active()` would return false so it probes nothing, satisfying the DoD; but epic rail 4 says anything this epic starts it stops, and an armed timer that can never fire usefully is something started and not stopped. Preference recorded: skip arming. The worker must decide explicitly rather than leave it unexamined.
planningNotes.codebaseInsights:
THIS ROW EXTENDS AN EXISTING MECHANISM; almost nothing here is new. All three call sites measured at HEAD:
- health-probe-ring.ts:240-245 — `createHealthProbeJob(options, dedicated)` enumerates `[...readDeployLedger(options.store, options.projectId).keys()].filter((name) => !skip.has(name))` where `skip = dedicated()` is called INSIDE the returned job, i.e. per tick. Its comment at :237-239 says so and says why: "setting or clearing an interval needs no restart; empty by default, which is the shipped behaviour."
- health-probe-ring.ts:249-252 — `createEnvironmentHealthProbeJob(options, environment, active)` returns `active() ? [environment] : []`, also per tick.
- health-probe-ring.ts:221 — `probeJob(options, environments)`'s own comment: "One ring, one abort contract, one failure code per tick; only the environment SOURCE differs." That is the axis this row changes and the only one.

THE COMPOSITION, daemon-store-foundation-composition.ts:641-675, is the template for the wiring: `probeIntervals` constructed ONCE at :641; `dedicated()` at :649 reads `probeIntervals.stored()` on EVERY call; `dedicatedJob(environment)` at :652 composes `() => dedicated().has(environment)` as the per-environment `active`; `reconcileProbeSchedules()` at :662 arms a schedule per interval-record entry; `sweepProbe` at :670; and :672-675 reconciles BEFORE sweeping so a newly-dedicated environment is not probed twice on the way to being right.

THE FAIL DIRECTION IS THE ONE REAL DESIGN DECISION, and it is NOT the same as the interval record's. :649's comment says an unreadable interval store yields the EMPTY set, "which hands every environment back to the sweep at the default rate — never no probing at all". Fail-open is right there because the cost is probing at the default rate. For RETIREMENT the two failure directions are: empty set → probe environments that may be retired (the defect this row fixes), or everything-retired → probe nothing (worse). Neither is free; step 1 forces the worker to choose and say why rather than inheriting the neighbour's answer by copy-paste.

THE DEDICATED-JOB ESCAPE is the clause a partial fix fails. An environment that owns an interval is served by `dedicatedJob`, NOT by the sweep, so excluding it from the sweep alone leaves it probing forever. Retirement has to reach `active()` too.

TEST SURFACES THAT ALREADY EXIST: health-probe-io.test.ts drives `createHealthProbeJob` directly with a fake `http` and asserts `fixture.ring.read(<name>)` (see :146-159, which deploys two environments and asserts both rings) — that is the idiom for the sweep arms. health-probe-schedule.test.ts is the neighbour covering the dedicated/reconcile path. There is NO test file for daemon-store-foundation-composition.ts, so the composed predicate is asserted by passing it to `createEnvironmentHealthProbeJob` directly rather than through the composition.

PREREQUISITE: `apps/daemon/src/monitoring/environment-retirement-record.ts` is child 1 (task-a2dd124fed1b4b9889c626824fc0a6fb) and does not exist yet. dependsOn gates WORKING claims until it lands, which is the correct enforcement — this plan names it as a prerequisite and does not plan around it.
planningNotes.risks:
1. THE PARTIAL FIX: excluding retired names from the SWEEP only. An environment that owns a dedicated interval is served by `dedicatedJob`, not the sweep, so it would keep probing forever — the exact defect this row exists to close, surviving in a narrower form. DoD 3 and drill (iii) hunt it.

2. A CAPTURED SET INSTEAD OF A PER-TICK READ. Reading the retirement snapshot once at job construction passes the obvious arm and fails silently in production, where the job outlives every retirement. Arm (b) and drill (ii) are the pair that catch it.

3. THE FAIL DIRECTION INHERITED BY COPY-PASTE. The interval record's fail-open (:649) is correct for intervals and is NOT automatically correct for retirement. An unexamined `?? new Set()` is a decision made by accident.

4. A FILTER THAT TAKES THE WHOLE LIST. Arm (c) — default behaviour unchanged with nothing retired — is what stops an over-broad exclusion passing every other arm.

5. THIS ROW LANDS A READER WITH NO WRITER, deliberately. Nothing can retire an environment until child 4 lands, so this change is observably inert on its own. That is the point (the capability is never advertised before it works) and it must be stated in the completion record so QA does not read it as an untested change.

6. `pnpm test` COVERS NONE OF THIS — the root vitest include has no `apps/**`. `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test` is the only leg that exercises these files.
